It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. What is GPU Leaderboard? GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: Inference pricing: a cost calculator for a full run, not a single hourly rate. Leaderboard : every offer ranked by $/GPU-hr, filterable by GPU, tier, region and availability. Cheapest Inference : the lowest on-demand floor for each tracked GPU. Providers : a directory with instance counts, regions, status-page incidents and price-check history. How does the GPU inference cost calculator work? You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. This is the number most budget sheets miss. What does the Deploy It Chrome extension do? GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It brings the price data to where developers pick models. Per its store listing, it works in 3 places: Hugging Face model pages: detects model size and estimates VRAM at FP16, INT8 and INT4. It then shows the cheapest hourly GPUs that fit. GitHub repos: detects model references and gives a hardware estimate in place. Toolbar lookup: search any model or GPU from the browser toolbar. Key Takeaways GPU Leaderboard ranks 201 live GPU offers from 24 providers by $/GPU-hr. Its calculator prices a full run, including idle time at your utilization. Deploy It shows VRAM needs and cheapest GPUs on Hugging Face and GitHub. An 8×H100, 72-hour run spans $967.68 to $3,545.28 across multiple providers. Coverage and daily refresh are the main gaps versus older trackers. Try it at gpuleaderboard.com and install the Deploy It extension from the Chrome Web Store. The post MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. It returns calibrated probabilities for up to 1,000 yes/no, choice and rubric questions over text, images, audio, video and PDFs, at $0.10 per 1M input tokens. The post Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API , powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 ( gemini-decision-1 ). The Gemini Decisions API does not generate text. It scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. For developers, this targets the small branching calls inside agents: routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. Google prices it at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with zero output tokens billed. TL;DR Size: Context is 262,144 tokens (256K) across shared input and all questions. Runs on: Google-hosted API only (Gemini Developer API, v1beta). No open weights or self-hosting. Performance: Leads 7 of 9 accuracy benchmarks in Google’s table, with the lowest calibration error. Best: 92.2% on JevBench (public split). Worst: 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, its lowest score. It also trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%). Bottom line: Best: multimodal, calibrated decisions in 150-250 ms. Worst: not the cheapest; Jev 1.14 costs $0.68 vs $0.88 on the shared suite. What is the Gemini Decisions API? Gemini Decision 1 is a specialized multimodal model from Google built for closed-set decisions. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one prefill pass. Output token usage is always 0. Your code branches directly on the returned numbers. Each request has 3 parts: a model ID, a shared input , and a map of questions. The docs define 3 question types: noul (yes/no): returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99. choice : picks 1 of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for every option. score : rates input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score. Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1. Google suggests routing low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer. Questions are scored in parallel and cannot see each other. How does Gemini Decision 1 work? Standard models decode an answer token by token, then your code parses it. Gemini Decision 1 instead scores your candidate options in one forward pass. Google reports median model compute of 50-100 ms and 150-250 ms end to end. That holds for inputs up to 16K tokens and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. Billing follows the same design. The shared input is billed once per request, however many questions you ask. Each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens. There are no thinking-token, transcription or OCR charges. Gemini Decision 1 benchmarks Google tested Gemini Decision 1 against 3 rivals. They are TypeSafe Jev 1.14 , GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI Decisions and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. All figures below are self-reported by Google. Refusals and safety blocks count as incorrect. Benchmark Gemini Decision 1 TypeSafe Jev 1.14 GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI Decisions) Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite JevBench (public split) 92.2% 90.0% 90.9% 86.6% Amazon ESCI (Macro-F1) 58.7% 56.7% 54.7% 47.2% New Yorker Caption (text-only) 79.7% 72.0% 68.4% 73.7% Mind2Web Multimodal 86.2% 86.8% 81.8% 78.0% PubMedQA 79.8% 78.2% 74.4% 77.6% Global-MMLU-Lite (non-English) 86.0% 85.0% 79.6% 78.8% When2Call 79.9% 82.0% 70.4% 60.9% MMAU (audio) 71.8% Not reported Not reported 67.7% Video-MME (no subtitles) 69.1% Not reported Not reported 63.3% Top-1 ECE (lower is better) 0.0250 0.0494 0.0721 0.2104 Total price, 7 shared evals $0.88 $0.68 $0.93 $4.14 Source: Google blog benchmark table . The calibration result is the clearest gap. Gemini Decision 1’s error of 0.0250 is about half of Jev 1.14’s 0.0494. That matters when you set confidence thresholds for automation. On cost, Google says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite across the shared suite ($0.88 vs $4.14). Gemini Decisions API vs OpenAI Decisions vs TypeSafe Jev Feature Gemini Decision 1 GPT-6 Luna, OpenAI Decisions TypeSafe Jev 1.14 Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Context 262,144 tokens 1,050,000 ( model page ) 64K per request, 262K with opt-in header Questions per request 1 to 1,000 1 to 400 No fixed cap, bounded by context Input modalities Text, image, audio, video, PDF Text, image, JSON Text (docs) Input price per 1M tokens $0.10 $0.10 uncached $0.042 Output price $0 $0 $0 Prompt caching Not supported Supported, charged at Luna rates Not disclosed Latency claim 150-250 ms end to end About 10x faster than Responses API Not disclosed How to deploy the Gemini Decisions API The endpoint is live on the Gemini Developer API (v1beta) and needs google-genai SDK 3.2 or later. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez . He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank . Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn , asking for career advice. It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own. Felipe Monsalve, Cipriano Echavarría and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, founders of Palomma. (Courtesy photo) Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma , has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned. The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital , Clocktower Technology Ventures , Tekton Ventures , Simma Capital and Yango Ventures , alongside existing investors Y Combinator , 17Sigma , Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures . Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume. The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority. “We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview. Finding a business in rent payments Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners. After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo , MIT -trained engineers with experience at Meta , Cobre and JP Morgan . The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent. It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said. Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties. The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled. From software to financial services Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products. From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The company is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments. Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services. Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The company reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less. Overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI , Bilt , TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business. Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products. “In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.” Managing the risk AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants. The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees. The startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría said. The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also plans to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions. Pepe Bolaños , managing partner at Cometa, said Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted. “We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email. Bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Tue, 10 Nov 2026 21:08:13 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 How Founders Can Reduce Platform Risk Before It Threatens Growth https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/startup-founders-reduce-platform-risk-filippenko-intch/ Thu, 12 Nov 2026 12:00:44 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94370 By Yakov Filippenko One day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work. For years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive. In 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery. It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too. Understand what a removal can take away Yakov Filippenko, founder and CEO at Intch. First, prospective customers can no longer download your app. Then, paying subscribers flood support with a more damaging question. “The app is gone. Are you a scam?” The bloodshed continues as existing users replace their phones and can’t reinstall the app, eroding your customer base. Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero. Before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you? If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control. Don’t make an appeal your contingency plan Cal AI , reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait. In Intch ’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection. Your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome. Build the alternative before you need it Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel. It also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov , founder of Telegram , has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship. The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront. We initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered. If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it. Include platform exposure in growth decisions Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business. Before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the company could survive an unanswered appeal. Investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions. Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it. You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your company. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice. Yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex , he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay , which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko launched Intch , an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles. Guided by our core values of Customer Obsession, Ownership, Curiosity, Humility, Efficiency, and Teamwork (COCHET), we are committed to delivering exceptional hospitality experiences to every guest. </p> <p>Smart Suites is an AI-driven company that continuously adopts and integrates advanced technology, automation, and digital tools to improve efficiency, decision-making, and customer satisfaction. We are looking for team members who are equally passionate about using AI tools, data-driven insights, and digital systems to strengthen operations and service delivery. </p> <p>At Smart Suites, we aim to ensure every guest stay is not only clean and comfortable, but also thoughtfully managed and personalized in a way that leaves a lasting impression. </p> <p><strong>Know how to spot a good used-car deal?</strong> </p> <p>We are looking for an experienced automotive professional to find vehicles overseas, primarily in Japan, and coordinate their import, preparation and resale in Australia. </p> <p>You will work remotely from the Philippines, partnering with auction agents, exporters, shipping providers and Australian mechanics and service providers. </p> <p><strong>What you will do</strong> </p> <ul><li>Find vehicles through auctions, dealers and exporter networks. </li></ul> <ul><li>Assess vehicle condition, repair needs and resale potential. </li></ul> <ul><li>Calculate total costs and recommend a maximum buying price. </li></ul> <ul><li>Coordinate imports, repairs, transport and preparation for sale. </li></ul> <ul><li>Manage listings, buyer follow-up and local handover arrangements. </li></ul> <ul><li>Track costs, progress and profit for each vehicle. </li></ul> <p><strong>What we are looking for</strong> </p> <ul><li>Experience in used-car buying, vehicle appraisal, automotive purchasing or vehicle trading. </li></ul> <ul><li>Practical knowledge of mechanical issues, accident damage and repair costs. </li></ul> <ul><li>Ability to interpret auction sheets and recognize risky purchases. </li></ul> <ul><li>Strong commercial judgement, organization and communication skills. </li></ul> <ul><li>Confidence working independently with spreadsheets and online tools. </li></ul> <p>Japanese auction experience is highly valued. Australian import knowledge is an advantage. Japanese fluency is helpful but not essential if you can reliably interpret and verify vehicle information. </p> <p><strong>What is on offer</strong> </p> <ul><li>Full-time work from home in the Philippines. </li></ul> <ul><li>Fixed monthly pay of 1,300 – 1,500 AUD, depending on experience. </li></ul> <ul><li>Commission equal to 5% of realized net profit per qualifying completed vehicle sale, subject to agreed terms. </li></ul> <ul><li>Opportunity to help build and grow an international vehicle trading operation. </li></ul> <p>Agreed availability during Australian and Japanese business hours is required. </p> <p><strong>To apply</strong> </p> <p>Send your CV and a short example of a vehicle you sourced, valued or purchased. Explain how you assessed its condition, buying price, expected costs and resale potential. The post Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API , powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 ( gemini-decision-1 ). The Gemini Decisions API does not generate text. It scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. For developers, this targets the small branching calls inside agents: routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. Google prices it at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with zero output tokens billed. TL;DR Size: Context is 262,144 tokens (256K) across shared input and all questions. Runs on: Google-hosted API only (Gemini Developer API, v1beta). No open weights or self-hosting. Performance: Leads 7 of 9 accuracy benchmarks in Google’s table, with the lowest calibration error. Best: 92.2% on JevBench (public split). Worst: 58.7% Macro-F1 on Amazon ESCI, its lowest score. It also trails Jev 1.14 on When2Call (79.9% vs 82.0%). Bottom line: Best: multimodal, calibrated decisions in 150-250 ms. Worst: not the cheapest; Jev 1.14 costs $0.68 vs $0.88 on the shared suite. What is the Gemini Decisions API? Gemini Decision 1 is a specialized multimodal model from Google built for closed-set decisions. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one prefill pass. Output token usage is always 0. Your code branches directly on the returned numbers. Each request has 3 parts: a model ID, a shared input , and a map of questions. The docs define 3 question types: noul (yes/no): returns the probability of yes, bounded between 0.01 and 0.99. choice : picks 1 of 2 to 255 options and returns normalized probabilities for every option. score : rates input on 2 to 255 ordered rubric levels and returns a probability-weighted score. Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1. Google suggests routing low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer. Questions are scored in parallel and cannot see each other. How does Gemini Decision 1 work? Standard models decode an answer token by token, then your code parses it. Gemini Decision 1 instead scores your candidate options in one forward pass. Google reports median model compute of 50-100 ms and 150-250 ms end to end. That holds for inputs up to 16K tokens and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. Billing follows the same design. The shared input is billed once per request, however many questions you ask. Each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens. There are no thinking-token, transcription or OCR charges. Gemini Decision 1 benchmarks Google tested Gemini Decision 1 against 3 rivals. They are TypeSafe Jev 1.14 , GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI Decisions and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. All figures below are self-reported by Google. Refusals and safety blocks count as incorrect. Benchmark Gemini Decision 1 TypeSafe Jev 1.14 GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI Decisions) Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite JevBench (public split) 92.2% 90.0% 90.9% 86.6% Amazon ESCI (Macro-F1) 58.7% 56.7% 54.7% 47.2% New Yorker Caption (text-only) 79.7% 72.0% 68.4% 73.7% Mind2Web Multimodal 86.2% 86.8% 81.8% 78.0% PubMedQA 79.8% 78.2% 74.4% 77.6% Global-MMLU-Lite (non-English) 86.0% 85.0% 79.6% 78.8% When2Call 79.9% 82.0% 70.4% 60.9% MMAU (audio) 71.8% Not reported Not reported 67.7% Video-MME (no subtitles) 69.1% Not reported Not reported 63.3% Top-1 ECE (lower is better) 0.0250 0.0494 0.0721 0.2104 Total price, 7 shared evals $0.88 $0.68 $0.93 $4.14 Source: Google blog benchmark table . The calibration result is the clearest gap. Gemini Decision 1’s error of 0.0250 is about half of Jev 1.14’s 0.0494. That matters when you set confidence thresholds for automation. On cost, Google says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite across the shared suite ($0.88 vs $4.14). A no-cost tier is available for prototyping in Google AI Studio . Python, JavaScript and REST guides are in the documentation . Ecosystem support is rolling out across OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel AI SDK , LiteLLM , Pydantic AI , Pipecat , LiveKit and OpenCode . Support in Gemini on Google Cloud is listed as coming soon. Google already uses it internally. Gemini Notebook routes queries to model tiers with it, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. It runs at 12.5 Hz with 12 codebooks and encodes about 361x faster than real time on a single CPU thread. The post Liquid AI Releases LiquidCodec, a 74M-Parameter Streaming Audio Codec appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Liquid AI has released LiquidCodec , the audio codec behind its LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B models. The LiquidCodec audio codec is a ~74M-parameter streaming speech tokenizer. It turns speech into tokens a language model can predict, then converts those tokens back into audio. Liquid AI had 2 goals: easy-to-predict tokens and fast conversion back to speech. The weights are on Hugging Face . TL;DR Size: ~74M parameters (73.6M on the model card ); 24 kHz audio, 12.5 Hz frames, 12 codebooks. Runs on: a single CPU thread (tested on an Apple M4 Max laptop, FP32); CUDA GPUs via Transformers; Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. Performance: best ViSQOL and lowest mel distance on all 8 test sets versus X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi. Best: ~361x real-time encoding on 1 CPU thread (encode RTF 0.0028 vs Mimi’s 0.0361). What is LiquidCodec? LiquidCodec is a Liquid AI speech codec that compresses 24 kHz audio into 12 token streams. Each 80 ms frame becomes 12 discrete tokens, per the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . It replaces Kyutai’s Mimi , which Liquid AI used in LFM2-Audio-1.5B. Mimi has 96.2M parameters. How does LiquidCodec work? The pipeline is encode, quantize, decode. Liquid AI uses blocks from its LFM3 architecture in both the encoder and decoder. The 2 halves are symmetric, and the encoder is fully causal, which suits streaming. Quantization uses grouped finite scalar quantization (GFSQ) instead of residual vector quantization (RVQ). In RVQ, each codebook encodes what the previous one missed. GFSQ groups are independent, so all 12 codebooks can be predicted in parallel by MaskGIT-style transformers. The decoder predicts spectral coefficients directly. This avoids learned transposed-convolution upsampling, a common cost in waveform decoders. How was it trained? Training ran in 2 stages. Stage 1 used 264,000 hours of speech across 107 languages. It applied waveform and spectral losses, without adversarial losses. Stage 2 fine-tuned on 55,000 hours of full-band speech (24 kHz or higher) with adversarial critics. Liquid AI says this removed metallic artifacts left after stage 1. A final decoder-only quantization-aware training (QAT) step targets edge inference. How fast is LiquidCodec? Liquid AI measured speed in FP32 on 1 CPU thread of an Apple M4 Max MacBook Pro. LiquidCodec ran at ~361x real time for encoding and ~87x for decoding. These are self-reported figures. Real-time factor (RTF) is processing time divided by audio length, so lower is better. LiquidCodec’s encode RTF is 0.0028, against 0.0361 for Mimi, 0.2145 for NanoCodec and 0.7359 for X-Codec 2. Decode RTF is 0.0115, against 0.0329, 0.2543 and 0.0379. That is about 13x lower encode RTF and 2.9x lower decode RTF than Mimi. How does LiquidCodec compare on quality benchmarks? Liquid AI used 8 test sets. These were LibriSpeech test-clean, Seed-TTS English and Mandarin, and 5 FLEURS languages (German, French, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean). Baselines were X-Codec 2, NanoCodec and Mimi at 12 codebooks. Reconstruction : LiquidCodec had the best ViSQOL and lowest mel distance on all 8 sets. On LibriSpeech, ViSQOL was 4.319 versus 4.219 (NanoCodec), 4.119 (X-Codec 2) and 4.031 (Mimi). Text-to-speech : Liquid AI trained identical TTS models on each codec’s tokens. Data (101,000 hours, 6 languages), architecture, compute and batch order were fixed. LiquidCodec scored the highest UTMOSv2 on all 8 sets and the best WER/CER on 4 of 8. LibriSpeech WER was 3.15%, against 6.27% for Mimi. Results held with a Qwen3-1.7B backbone as well as LFM3-1.7B. Where it trails : NanoCodec scored higher PESQ (WB) on 7 of 8 sets. It also led on LibriSpeech speaker similarity (SECS 0.836 vs 0.785). LiquidCodec vs Mimi vs NanoCodec vs X-Codec 2 Feature LiquidCodec Mimi NanoCodec 1.78 kbps X-Codec 2 Developer Liquid AI Kyutai NVIDIA HKUST Audio Parameters 73.6M 96.2M 62M 0.8B Sample rate 24 kHz 24 kHz ( repo ) 22.05 kHz 16 kHz Frame rate 12.5 Hz 12.5 Hz 12.5 fps 50 tokens/s Codebooks 12 8 at 1.1 kbps ( blog ) 13 1 ( docs ) Quantizer GFSQ RVQ ( docs ) FSQ Single-layer FSQ ( docs ) Bitrate Not disclosed 1.1 kbps 1.78 kbps Not disclosed Causality Causal encoder; decoder not disclosed Fully causal ( Kyutai ) Non-causal encoder, causal decoder Not disclosed License “other” on HF; blog links LFM License CC-BY 4.0 NVIDIA Open Model License CC-BY-NC 4.0 Encode / decode RTF, M4 Max CPU* 0.0028 / 0.0115 0.0361 / 0.0329 0.2145 / 0.2543 0.7359 / 0.0379 LibriSpeech mel distance* (lower is better) 0.120 0.160 0.122 0.123 LibriSpeech PESQ (WB)* 2.640 2.615 2.942 2.434 LibriSpeech TTS UTMOSv2* 3.31 2.89 3.19 3.27 *Measured by Liquid AI in its LiquidCodec blog . Mimi measured at 12 codebooks. How can developers deploy LiquidCodec? The codec loads through Hugging Face Transformers with trust_remote_code=True . Call encode() to get audio codes and decode() to get a waveform. A native LiquidCodecStreamingCache supports chunk-by-chunk decoding, per the model card . The card’s examples use CUDA with bfloat16. For edge use, Liquid AI lists Q4_0, Q4_K_M and Q8_0 GGUF builds for llama.cpp. GGUF repos ship with LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B . Q4_0 with decoder-only QAT shrinks the decoder footprint by 3.5x. LibriSpeech ViSQOL dips only from 4.319 to 4.292. Key Takeaways ~74M-parameter streaming codec, 12.5 Hz, 12 codebooks, 24 kHz. ~361x real-time encode, ~87x decode on 1 CPU thread. Best ViSQOL, mel distance and TTS UTMOSv2 on all 8 test sets. NanoCodec still wins PESQ (WB) on 7 of 8 sets. Q4_0 decoder is 3.5x smaller with minimal quality loss. newContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Hadley Designs LLC: Amazon Brand Manager Anywhere in the World Texas Paid Social Media Advertising, Product Marketing, Product Lifecycle Management, Power BI/Tableau, Product Listing, and Amazon Seller Central Sales and Marketing Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/6760/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Flower Mound, TX, USA <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="http://www.hadleydesigns.com">http://www.hadleydesigns.com</a> </p> <div> <p><strong>Own Your Catalog Like a Business, and Win on Amazon.</strong></p> <p>Hadley Designs is seeking an Amazon Brand Manager to take full ownership of a multi-million dollar group of our products on Amazon, as the product manager, the merchandiser, and the CEO of that catalog. This is a high-impact role for an e-commerce brand builder who brings real judgment, reads a market quickly, and knows how to grow net profit, not just sales.</p> <p>You will report to the leader of our Amazon channel and work as part of a small, high-performing Amazon team. While this role operates deeply within Amazon, we welcome candidates who have built brands across e-commerce, DTC, or marketplace environments and are excited to bring that experience to a scaled Amazon catalog.</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p><strong>How You'll Win at Hadley Designs</strong></p> <p>You bring the judgment. We bring the brand, the catalog, and the team.</p> <ul> <li>Learn our brand. Get to know our brand, our expectations, your catalog group, and the standards and SOPs our team runs on.</li> <li>Run your catalog as its CEO.
